item.title: The anatomy of a personal health agent
item.dc:creator: A. Ali Heydari
Ken Gu
Vidya Srinivas
Hong Yu
Akshay Paruchuri
Zhihan Zhang
Yuwei Zhang
Qian He
item.description:
Authors: A. Ali Heydari, Ken Gu, Vidya Srinivas, Hong Yu, Akshay Paruchuri, Zhihan Zhang, Yuwei Zhang, Qian He, et al.
Journal: Nature
Abstract: Abstract Large language models are enabling a new generation of health agents, yet their ability to address the diverse needs of individuals in everyday health settings remains underexplored 1,2 . Here we developed a comprehensive personal health agent that reasons over multimodal data from consumer wellness devices and medical records to provide personalized health support. Through analysis of web search and health forum queries, together with user-centred research involving end users and health experts, we identified four key user journeys: general health knowledge, personal data interpretation, wellness advice, and symptom assessment. These journeys informed three specialist sub-agents: (1) a data science agent that analyses longitudinal wearable and medical data, incorporating population-level statistics to contextualize numerical insights; (2) a health domain expert agent that integrates personal and contextual data with health knowledge to generate personalized insights; and (3) a health coach agent that synthesizes insights, supports multi-turn interaction and goal setting, applies specified psychological strategies and tracks progress. We integrated these capabilities in the personal health agent, an open-source multi-agent framework for dynamic, personalized health interactions. We evaluated the sub-agents and full system across 11 benchmark tasks using automated and human evaluation, with more than 7,000 annotations and 1,350 h of effort from health experts and end users. This represents the most comprehensive evaluation of a personal health agent thus far and provides a concrete foundation for improving access to high-quality personalized health support more broadly.

item.title: WEE1 opposes APC/CCDH1 activity to promote S phase entry
item.dc:creator: Luc-Alban Vuillemenot
Lucas G. Morales
Calin-Mihai Dragoi
Betheney R. Pennycook
Edward Harris
Liuyang C. Lin
William A. Weston
Jade-Ellen Brown
item.description:
Authors: Luc-Alban Vuillemenot, Lucas G. Morales, Calin-Mihai Dragoi, Betheney R. Pennycook, Edward Harris, Liuyang C. Lin, William A. Weston, Jade-Ellen Brown, et al.
Journal: Nature
Abstract: Abstract WEE1 phosphorylates and inhibits the activity of cyclin-dependent kinases to prevent mitotic entry and establish a G2 DNA damage checkpoint 1–3 . Consequently, WEE1 inhibitors have been developed to be synthetically lethal in TP53- mutated tumours that become reliant on this WEE1-mediated checkpoint, and such inhibitors are undergoing clinical trials. However, WEE1 inhibitors also have efficacy in TP53- wild-type tumours, and many trials have been terminated owing to high levels of toxic side effects, suggesting that WEE1 has unknown functions. Here we show that WEE1 promotes cell cycle re-entry from quiescence (G0) by opposing the activity of the E3 ubiquitin ligase, anaphase-promoting complex–cyclosome bound to CDH1 (APC/C CDH1 ). WEE1 phosphorylates CDH1 ( FZR1 ) at key residues that mediate the interaction between CDH1 and APC/C. Cells with loss of function of WEE1 during G0/G1 have delayed S phase entry, impaired G1/S transition, abnormal S phase accumulation of cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor p21 Cip1/Kip1 and a p21-dependent G2 arrest. Reduced expression of APC/C CDH1 or p21 renders cells more sensitive to acute WEE1 inhibition, and both pathways are downregulated in cells with acquired WEE1 inhibitor resistance. These results reveal a mechanism of cell cycle control that has implications for how WEE1 inhibitors should be used in the clinic.

item.title: Cold activates a BH2 metabolic network promoting longevity and proteostasis
item.dc:creator: Hyun Ju Lee
Cansu Doğan
Seda Koyuncu
Markus Wehrmann
Murat Artan
Dunja Petrovic
Rute Loureiro
Amit Kumar Sahu
item.description:
Authors: Hyun Ju Lee, Cansu Doğan, Seda Koyuncu, Markus Wehrmann, Murat Artan, Dunja Petrovic, Rute Loureiro, Amit Kumar Sahu, et al.
Journal: Nature
Abstract: Abstract Moderately cold temperatures extend lifespan and promote health across species 1–3 , yet the molecular mechanisms underlying these benefits remain unclear. Here we define a metabolite-driven, multi-tissue signalling system that links cold temperature to enhanced longevity and proteostasis in Caenorhabditis elegans . Cold temperature upregulates the biopterin-synthesis enzyme CAT-4 (GCH1 in humans), increasing production of dihydrobiopterin (BH2), a transportable reservoir for the bioactive cofactor tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4). BH2 is produced in muscle and transported to distal tissues, including the intestine and neurons, where it is converted into BH4 by the salvage enzyme DHFR-1. BH4 functions as an essential cofactor for phenylalanine hydroxylase PAH-1, promoting tyrosine synthesis and extending lifespan. This BH2–BH4 axis also prevents disease-related protein aggregation and subsequent neuronal dysfunction during ageing. Importantly, increasing BH2 synthesis specifically in muscle is sufficient to promote longevity and suppress pathological protein aggregation in distal tissues, even at normal or elevated temperatures. In human cells, BH2 or tyrosine supplementation reduces aggregation of polyQ-expanded proteins associated with Huntington’s disease, as well as mutant variants of TDP-43 and FUS that cause amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. Together, these findings identify BH2 as a cold-induced metabolite of which the synthesis, intertissue transport and conversion into bioactive BH4 preserve organism-wide proteostasis and extend lifespan.

item.title: Drought and disease trigger novel interactions among top predators
item.dc:creator: Fabrizio Sergio
Haruki Natsukawa
Alessandro Tanferna
Javier Chicano
Francisco Carro
Ramón C. Soriguer
Fernando Hiraldo
Julio Blas
item.description:
Authors: Fabrizio Sergio, Haruki Natsukawa, Alessandro Tanferna, Javier Chicano, Francisco Carro, Ramón C. Soriguer, Fernando Hiraldo, Julio Blas
Journal: Nature
Abstract: Abstract Interactions among species are increasingly recognized as key determinants of climate change impacts on ecosystems 1–5 . However, we know little about how climatic perturbations affect interactions among top vertebrate predators. Here we show that, when an emergent disease caused the decline of shared prey (rabbits), after decades of neutral co-existence a mammalian carnivore (lynx) started to prey heavily on a top predatory raptor (kites). These predation bouts occurred exclusively under drought conditions and when lynx found rabbit remains under the raptor nests, consistent with the removal of a potential competitor. Drought-induced lynx predation depressed lifetime reproductive success and triggered territory abandonment and dispersal by the raptor, suggestive of a new arms race among predators. A reduction in raptor abundance was associated with an increase in an insectivorous bird (a small owl), showing that the new interaction had the potential to reach lower trophic levels. These results underline the importance of diet flexibility and mobility as important mediators of resilience to stressors. In the future, synergistic effects of multiple anthropogenic stressors may reshape the interactions and ecological roles of many apex predators, with potential cascading consequences for whole ecosystems. A key to forecasting the future impact of global change may reside in understanding how behavioural flexibility and interacting keystone species respond to interacting shocks.

item.title: Amazon carbon emissions driven by human actions amplified by droughts
item.dc:creator: Luciana V. Gatti
Camilla L. Cunha
Juan C. G. Blas
A. Scott Denning
Mariane S. Reis
Luciano Marani
Egidio Arai
Cassiano Gustavo Messias
item.description:
Authors: Luciana V. Gatti, Camilla L. Cunha, Juan C. G. Blas, A. Scott Denning, Mariane S. Reis, Luciano Marani, Egidio Arai, Cassiano Gustavo Messias, et al.
Journal: Nature
Abstract: Abstract The Amazon carbon sink is weakening as deforestation 1–5 , rising tree mortality 6–8 and climate change disrupt the climatic conditions that sustain a humid tropical forest 9–11 . Forest loss reduces precipitation, increases temperatures and lengthens the dry season, driving higher carbon emissions 1–4,11,12 . Climate stress is stronger in more deforested regions, rendering forests progressively more flammable 1,9,13 . Large-scale climate events, such as El Niño, further amplify regional climate impacts 9,14–17 . Here we present an analysis of 15 years of Amazonian carbon fluxes derived from atmospheric CO 2 measurements. We determine a carbon balance of 0.32 ± 0.08 PgC yr −1 , with fires acting as the dominant source (0.40 ± 0.07 PgC yr −1 ) and forest uptake becoming increasingly unable to offset emissions. Furthermore, we investigate key drivers of the carbon emissions of Amazonia and identify three distinct year groups. Group 1 (2011–2014, 2017 and 2018) represents the role of the Amazon in the global carbon balance (0.11 ± 0.08 PgC yr −1 ) during wetter years with low human activity, such as deforestation, biomass burning and degradation. Group 2 (2019–2022) represents Amazon carbon emissions (0.43 ± 0.13 PgC yr −1 ) from human activities (mainly deforestation and degradation) during years with low climatic stress. Group 3 (2010, 2015, 2016, 2023 and 2024) has the highest carbon emissions (0.49 ± 0.07 PgC yr −1 ) and comprises warm and dry years (high climate stress), such as El Niño and the warming of the Tropical North Atlantic Ocean, associated with biomass burning.

item.title: Enzyme-embedded polyesters for accelerated biodegradation in the deep sea
item.dc:creator: QiuYuan Huang
Noriko Iida
Noriyuki Isobe
Taizo Kabe
Taku Omura
Manikandan Ilangovan
Satoshi Kimura
Jin Ho Seok
item.description:
Authors: QiuYuan Huang, Noriko Iida, Noriyuki Isobe, Taizo Kabe, Taku Omura, Manikandan Ilangovan, Satoshi Kimura, Jin Ho Seok, et al.
Journal: Nature
Abstract: Abstract The accumulation of persistent plastics in the ocean is causing wide-ranging environmental problems 1–3 . Some commercially available compostable plastics 4–7 , developed to address these issues, degrade efficiently under industrial composting conditions; however, their degradation in marine environments, particularly in the deep sea, remains limited 8–10 . Here we demonstrate that thermally embedding enzymes into compostable polyesters (poly(butylene succinate) (PBS), poly(butylene succinate- co -adipate) (PBSA), poly(ε-caprolactone) (PCL) and poly(butylene adipate- co -terephthalate) (PBAT)) significantly accelerates their degradation in both coastal and deep-sea environments from water depths of 2–6 m to 5,503 m. Enzyme-embedded polyesters achieved near-complete degradation at a deep-sea depth of 757 m within 5 months. Furthermore, moderate biodegradation of enzyme-embedded polyesters was observed under extreme conditions on deep-sea floors of 5,503 m. In coastal seawater, films embedded with trace amounts (0.1 wt%) of enzyme underwent rapid degradation. The mechanical properties of enzyme-embedded polyesters were similar to those of enzyme-free polyesters. Chemical analysis confirmed the formation of low-molecular-mass degradation products and biochemical oxygen demand measurements supported the mineralization of the enzyme-embedded polyesters. The enzyme-embedding strategy enables enhanced marine degradation of compostable polyesters and represents a potential solution to marine plastic pollution.
